newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions to clash with employers on sick pay.
newsitem.headline: German unions to clash with employers on sick pay.

text.p: German trade unions and employers were set on a collision course on Wednesday over the future of Germany's generous sick pay agreements, which may now be scrapped as part of Bonn's austerity package.

Unions have received qualified backing from employment law experts for their argument that new laws passed on Friday cannot replace hard-won agreements that guarantee workers 100 percent of their pay even during long-term illness.
But economists and other observers believe that if no legal agreement can be reached, unions could find public support crucially lacking if they then resort to strike action.

Confrontation in one of Germany's main industrial sectors flared on Wednesday as the Gesamtmetall group of metal and electronics sector employers defended its decision to urge member firms to scrap existing sick pay deals from next month.

"The fact is the new law comes into effect from October 1 and we must inform our member companies how they should act...We also must not shy away from this legal confrontation," Gesamtmetall chief Werner Stumpfe told German radio.
The new austerity measures allow German firms, who argue that sick pay is one of a number of employment costs making them uncompetitive, to cut sick pay to 80 percent of wages.
Backed by government ministers, they argue that even left-leaning countries such as Sweden have reduced sick pay to 75 percent of gross salaries.

But Ursula Engelen-Kefer, deputy head of the DGB trade union federation, insisted the vast majority of sick pay pacts for the 3.5 million workers in the metal and electronics sector were legally protected as separate clauses in wage contracts.
"To cut sick pay would be a clear breach of contract", Engelen-Kefer, also speaking on radio, said.
Initial soundings from German employment law experts appeared to support the union's case.

Thomas Dietrich, president of the Federal Industrial Tribunal, said on German television that if a 100 percent sick pay clause was expressly mentioned in a wage contract, "the most favourable (interpretation) should go to the worker".

But if no specific percentage figure had been included in wage contracts -- which could apply to most workers in the construction and chemical sectors -- courts could rule that the new sick pay measures should apply, he added.
Gesamtmetall's Stumpfe described Dietrich's intervention as a "scandalous" pre-judgement.

Amid uncertainty over the application of the new laws, unions from IG Metall to white-collar workers' group DAG have confirmed their readiness to consider strikes as a means of defending sick pay deals in existing and future contracts.

But observers of German industrial relations are increasingly convinced that the way Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government has handled austerity measures, which are due to shave some 70 billion marks ($46.24 billion) from public spending next year, means public support for the unions could be limited.

"Look at the local elections at the weekend, where even after the austerity package the CDU lost relatively little ground," Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at the German subsidiary of Swiss bank UBS said, referring to the main coalition party's lead in local elections in the state of Lower Saxony.

"The government has said: 'We have to cut spending to promote growth' -- and it seems a few people have believed them," he added, also noting a recent poll showing a majority of Germans accepting the need for cost-cutting.

Mark Cliffe, chief international economist at London-based Midland Global Markets, said Kohl had perhaps correctly judged he was in a strong enough position to force through such measures, vital to German entry into European Monetary Union.
"The opposition SPD tried to promote an anti-EMU theme in (Baden-Wuerttemberg state) elections in March and went backwards. That's quite a telling episode," Cliffe said. ($1=1.5138 Mark)
